questiontext.text:
A child-health programme is being evaluated using a survey in Kenya. Each row of your dataset represents one child. Children belong to households; households belong to survey clusters; clusters are located within counties. Each cluster received Programme A or Programme B.

Download your CSV dataset. Use the statistical software of your choice to explore it.

Construct the overall graph

For each programme, find the proportion of children who are fully vaccinated (fully_vaccinated = 1). Move the two sliders to change the bar heights. The bars show percentages, not the total number vaccinated: each programme may have a different number of children.

[[jsxgraph width="100%" aspect-ratio="1.9/1" input-ref-ans1="aRef" input-ref-ans2="bRef"]] var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid,{ boundingbox:[-0.55,117,3.25,-27],axis:false, showCopyright:false,showNavigation:false, pan:{enabled:false},zoom:{enabled:false} }); var blue='#4285c5',red='#e57373'; for(var y=0;y<=100;y+=20){ board.create('segment',[[0.28,y],[2.85,y]],{strokeColor:'#dddddd',dash:2,fixed:true}); board.create('text',[-0.10,y,y+'%'],{fontSize:12,fixed:true,anchorX:'right'}); } var sa=board.create('slider',[[0.60,-13],[1.42,-13],[0,50,100]],{ name:'',snapWidth:0.5,strokeColor:blue,fillColor:blue, baseline:{strokeColor:blue},highline:{strokeColor:blue} }); var sb=board.create('slider',[[1.66,-13],[2.48,-13],[0,50,100]],{ name:'',snapWidth:0.5,strokeColor:red,fillColor:red, baseline:{strokeColor:red},highline:{strokeColor:red} }); stack_jxg.bind_slider(aRef,sa); stack_jxg.bind_slider(bRef,sb); function bar(x,s,c){ board.create('polygon',[ [x-0.29,0],[x+0.29,0], [x+0.29,function(){return s.Value();}], [x-0.29,function(){return s.Value();}] ],{fillColor:c,fillOpacity:0.85, borders:{strokeColor:c},vertices:{visible:false},fixed:true,highlight:false}); board.create('text',[x,function(){return s.Value()+5;}, function(){return s.Value().toFixed(1)+'%';}], {fontSize:15,anchorX:'middle',fixed:true,highlight:false}); } bar(1,sa,blue);bar(2,sb,red); board.create('text',[1,-23,'Programme A'],{anchorX:'middle',fontSize:14,fixed:true}); board.create('text',[2,-23,'Programme B'],{anchorX:'middle',fontSize:14,fixed:true}); board.update(); [[/jsxgraph]]

Complete the graph within wealth quintiles

The blue bars already show Programme A's vaccination rates in each wealth quintile. Use your dataset to find Programme B's rates and move the five red sliders to complete the graph. Each bar shows the percentage vaccinated within that programme and quintile, not the number of children. Aim for the nearest percentage point.

[[jsxgraph width="100%" aspect-ratio="1.65/1" input-ref-ans4="r1" input-ref-ans5="r2" input-ref-ans6="r3" input-ref-ans7="r4" input-ref-ans8="r5"]] var board=JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid,{ boundingbox:[0,119,6.15,-29],axis:false,showCopyright:false, showNavigation:false,pan:{enabled:false},zoom:{enabled:false} }); var a=[{#float(ta4)#},{#float(ta6)#},{#float(ta8)#},{#float(ta10)#},{#float(ta12)#}]; var refs=[r1,r2,r3,r4,r5]; var blue='#4285c5',red='#e57373'; for(var y=0;y<=100;y+=20){ board.create('segment',[[0.6,y],[5.75,y]],{strokeColor:'#dddddd',dash:2,fixed:true}); board.create('text',[0.45,y,y+'%'],{fontSize:11,anchorX:'right',fixed:true}); } function bar(x,h,c){ board.create('polygon',[[x-0.17,0],[x+0.17,0], [x+0.17,h],[x-0.17,h]],{ fillColor:c,fillOpacity:0.88,borders:{strokeColor:c}, vertices:{visible:false},fixed:true,highlight:false }); } for(var i=0;i<5;i++){ (function(i){ var x=i+1; bar(x-0.19,a[i],blue); board.create('text',[x-0.19,a[i]+4,a[i].toFixed(1)+'%'],{ fontSize:10,anchorX:'middle',fixed:true,highlight:false }); var s=board.create('slider',[[x-0.32,-14],[x+0.32,-14],[0,50,100]],{ name:'',snapWidth:0.5,strokeColor:red,fillColor:red, baseline:{strokeColor:red},highline:{strokeColor:red} }); stack_jxg.bind_slider(refs[i],s); bar(x+0.19,function(){return s.Value();},red); board.create('text',[x+0.19,function(){return s.Value()+4;}, function(){return s.Value().toFixed(1)+'%';}],{ fontSize:10,anchorX:'middle',fixed:true,highlight:false }); board.create('text',[x,-23,'Q'+(i+1)],{ fontSize:13,anchorX:'middle',fixed:true }); })(i); } board.create('text',[3,111,'Blue: Programme A (given) Red: Programme B (move sliders)'],{ fontSize:12,anchorX:'middle',fixed:true }); board.update(); [[/jsxgraph]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explore the results: what changes when we look within groups?

Overall: Programme A has {@A_total_vacc@} vaccinated children out of {@A_total_n@} ({@float(round(10*ta1)/10)@}%). Programme B has {@B_total_vacc@} out of {@B_total_n@} ({@float(round(10*ta2)/10)@}%). Programme A has the higher overall rate.

Within wealth quintiles: Programme B has the higher vaccination rate in every quintile. You can see the exact percentages below.

Wealth quintileProgramme AProgramme B
1{@float(round(10*ta4)/10)@}%{@float(round(10*ta5)/10)@}%
2{@float(round(10*ta6)/10)@}%{@float(round(10*ta7)/10)@}%
3{@float(round(10*ta8)/10)@}%{@float(round(10*ta9)/10)@}%
4{@float(round(10*ta10)/10)@}%{@float(round(10*ta11)/10)@}%
5{@float(round(10*ta12)/10)@}%{@float(round(10*ta13)/10)@}%

Explore the distribution of children

Before reading the explanation, compare the numbers of children in each quintile. Where are the two programmes most heavily represented?

[[jsxgraph width="100%" aspect-ratio="1.8/1"]] var A = [ {#A_n1#}, {#A_n2#}, {#A_n3#}, {#A_n4#}, {#A_n5#} ]; var B = [ {#B_n1#}, {#B_n2#}, {#B_n3#}, {#B_n4#}, {#B_n5#} ]; var maxN = Math.max.apply(null, A.concat(B)); var top = Math.ceil(maxN/100)*100+60; var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, { boundingbox: [-0.7, top, 6.1, -top*0.22], axis: false, showCopyright: false, showNavigation: false, pan: {enabled: false}, zoom: {enabled: false} }); var blue = '#4285c5'; var red = '#e57373'; function txt(x,y,s,size,bold) { return board.create('text',[x,y,s],{ fontSize:size, fixed:true, highlight:false, anchorX:'middle', anchorY:'middle', cssStyle:bold?'font-weight:bold;':'' }); } function bar(x,n,color) { board.create('polygon',[ [x-0.19,0], [x+0.19,0], [x+0.19,n], [x-0.19,n] ],{ fillColor:color, fillOpacity:0.9, borders:{strokeColor:color}, vertices:{visible:false}, fixed:true, highlight:false }); } var step = Math.ceil(maxN/5/50)*50; for (var y=0; y<=maxN; y+=step) { board.create('segment',[[0.3,y],[5.7,y]],{ strokeColor:'#dddddd', dash:2, fixed:true }); txt(-0.25,y,String(y),11,false); } for (var i=0; i<5; i++) { var x=i+1; bar(x-0.21,A[i],blue); bar(x+0.21,B[i],red); txt(x-0.21,A[i]+top*0.035, String(A[i]),11,true); txt(x+0.21,B[i]+top*0.035, String(B[i]),11,true); txt(x,-top*0.07,'Quintile '+(i+1),12,true); } txt(3,-top*0.16, 'Blue: Programme A Red: Programme B', 13,false); [[/jsxgraph]]

Why does the comparison reverse? Programme A has many more children in the wealthier quintiles, where vaccination rates tend to be higher for both programmes. Programme B has more children in the less wealthy quintiles. When everyone is combined, the two programmes therefore have very different mixes of children. This is an example of Simpson's paradox.

What does this tell us about levels of data?

What does this tell us about levels of data? The dataset contains children (individual level), households, survey clusters and counties. A child's vaccination status is recorded for that child; wealth is a household characteristic; the programme is assigned at cluster level. Children in the same household or cluster can share circumstances, so they should not automatically be thought of as completely unrelated observations. Looking only at the overall figures can hide important patterns within groups.

Remember: Wealth quintiles are the groups that reveal the reversal here. Children, households, clusters and counties are the levels describing how the dataset is organised. Both ways of looking at the data matter.

To calculate a percentage if you need it: (number vaccinated ÷ total number of children in that group) × 100. The denominator must match the group you are describing.
